message.content: The world had no horizon, only the endless, bleeding collision of color and form, and within that chaos, a single creature with round spectacles on a narrow nose was the only thing that cast a shadow. His name was Quill, though no one had named him, for there was no one. There was only the sky, which was not a sky but a vast canvas of smeoched cerulean and violent ochre, swirled by a brush that had no hand. The ground beneath his tiny, spined feet was not dirt or stone but a thick impasto of crimson and violet, ridged and textured like a fingerprint pressed into wet oil. Quill adjusted his glasses—thin wire rims, slightly crooked, held together with a wisp of tape—and peered ahead. The landscape did not repeat. It did not obey. A tree, if you could call it that, was a dripping spiral of magenta and gold, its "branches" merely the gestural flicks of a brush that had grown impatient. A river was a thick, undulating stroke of cobalt, frozen mid-sweep. Nothing moved. Nothing breathed. Everything was a painting of itself, beautiful and utterly inert. In a world made of pigment and gesture, the small, warm, breathing thing was not merely out of place; it was an error the brush had not yet corrected. Quill walked, and the walking was a small, stubborn act of rebellion. His quills rasped against the impasto ground. He blinked. His nose twitched, and the twitch sent a faint, real scent of damp earth into a world that smelled only of turpentine and linseed. He paused to examine a "boulder" that was actually a thick dab of titanium white shaped like a sphere. He touched it. It was flat. It was *paint*. He pulled his hand back, as though it had burned him, and adjusted his glasses again, because in a world of suggestion and symbol, seeing things as they truly were required a kind of courage. He was the only creature with a heartbeat, the only one who bled, the only one who would, in time, stop. The strokes around him did not age. The spiral-tree did not shed. The cobalt river did not dry. Quill's paws, however, grew dusty. The hedgehog understood, in the quiet arithmetic of his small heart, that his aloneness was not a wound but a witness. He sat beneath the magenta spiral-tree, which was not a tree, and he watched the way the colors bled into one another at their edges, the way the brush had layered one emotion over another until the whole sky looked like a feeling someone had tried to describe in a language made of pigment. He thought about what it must mean to be the only real thing in a world of beautiful abstraction. He thought that perhaps the world had been painted by someone who had looked at a hedgehog, a small, round, *true* little creature, and then, in the act of remembering, had lost it. Painted the whole vast, gorgeous landscape around the shape of where the hedgehog had been, and in the filling-in, forgot to fill him back in. So here he sat, the only subject that had not been flattened, the only figure with depth, with a second dimension, with a *third*. He wore his crooked glasses and he breathed, and his small breath fogged the lenses, and the fog cleared, and the world remained. To be the only real thing in a painted world is not to be lost; it is to be the proof that the painting was, once, a place. Quill stood. He picked up a pebble, and it was a pebble, not a dab of umber, and he rolled it a few inches along the impasto ground. It made a sound. A small, true, *real* sound, like a grain of rice hitting a wooden table. The cobalt river did not ripple. The magenta spiral did not turn. But the sound was there, and it was his, and it belonged to no brush. He walked on, his spines catching the flat, sourceless light, his glasses reflecting the smear of color in two small, round, *true* mirrors. Behind him, the impasto ground held the impression of his tiny footprints, the only texture in the world that was not painted. The only evidence that something had been here. The only evidence that the world, for all its beautiful, abstract silence, had once, before the first stroke, been *real*.
